overview: Topic 1.2 showed that quantum computers are specialised machines: they help only when a problem's structure lets interference concentrate probability on correct answers. Topic 1.3 asks the practical question: which problems are those, and where do things stand?

Four areas dominate the discussion. Cryptography: Shor's algorithm would let a large, error-corrected quantum computer break the public-key systems (RSA, elliptic-curve cryptography) that protect most internet traffic today. The response, post-quantum cryptography (PQC), is a new set of classical algorithms believed to resist quantum attack, and standards for them already exist. Simulation: nature is quantum, so molecules and materials are natural targets; a quantum computer can represent a quantum system's state without the exponential memory cost a classical computer pays (Topic 1.2, C06). Search and sampling: Grover's algorithm gives a provable but only quadratic speedup for unstructured search, and related techniques give quadratic speedups for some estimation tasks. Optimization and machine learning: these are heavily advertised, but clear, proven speedups for practical problems are much rarer, and many claims are still being tested.

Two realities frame everything. First, almost all of the big applications need fault-tolerant quantum computers — machines far larger and more reliable than the noisy devices available now. Second, in this fast-moving field claims of "quantum advantage" are regularly challenged by improved classical algorithms. A good learner knows what is proven, what is plausible, and what is hype.

Why the learner needs this: it turns the abstract ideas of Topics 1.1–1.2 into concrete reasons to care about quantum computing, and it protects against both over-hype ("quantum solves everything") and over-dismissal ("it's all fake").
Where it fits: it closes the introductory unit. Later topics on gates, circuits and algorithms (e.g. Grover, Shor) will point back to the applications here as motivation.

Connection to Topics 1.1–1.2: 1.2 introduced the capabilities (superposition, interference, entanglement, exponential state space) and the limits (measurement returns n bits; no known efficient solution to NP-complete problems). 1.3 maps those capabilities and limits onto real problems.

After this topic the learner can: explain the "quantum threat" to encryption accurately, say why chemistry is the flagship use case, estimate Grover speedups, and critically read news about quantum advantage.
• n qubits are described by 2ⁿ amplitudes, but measuring returns only n classical bits.
• Interference lets algorithms make correct answers more likely before measurement.
• Quantum speedups are problem-specific: Shor (factoring) is believed to be a large speedup;
Grover (unstructured search) is quadratic and provably optimal for that task.
• No efficient quantum algorithm for NP-complete problems is known.
• Today's quantum devices are noisy; large reliable computations need error correction.

mathematical_foundations: 6. Mathematical Foundations
EQUATION: Iterations ≈ (π/4)·√N
NAME: Grover iteration count (one marked item)
MEANING: Approximate number of Grover iterations to find one marked item among N.
VARIABLES: N = size of the search space.
WHY IT MATTERS: Quantifies the quadratic speedup.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Search time grows like the square root of the list size instead of the list size.
EQUATION: Effective quantum search cost of a k-bit key ≈ 2^(k/2)
NAME: Grover effect on symmetric keys (idealised)
MEANING: A k-bit key space of size 2ᵏ is searched in about 2^(k/2) steps.
VARIABLES: k = key length in bits.
WHY IT MATTERS: Explains why doubling key length restores security against Grover.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: The attacker's work is halved in the exponent; a 256-bit key behaves like a 128-bit key.
EXAMPLE: AES-256 → ≈ 2¹²⁸ (E02).
EQUATION: Number of amplitudes = 2ⁿ ;  memory ≈ 2ⁿ × 16 bytes (double-precision complex)
NAME: State-vector size
MEANING: Memory to store a general n-qubit state classically.
VARIABLES: n = number of qubits (or orbitals).
WHY IT MATTERS: Shows why direct classical simulation of larger quantum systems fails.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Each added qubit doubles the memory.
EXAMPLE: n = 50 → 16 PiB (E03).
EQUATION: E(θ) = ⟨ψ(θ)| H |ψ(θ)⟩ ≥ E₀
NAME: Variational principle
MEANING: Any trial state's average energy is at least the true lowest energy E₀.
VARIABLES: θ = adjustable parameters; H = Hamiltonian (energy operator); E₀ = ground-state energy.
WHY IT MATTERS: Justifies minimising E(θ) to approach the ground state (VQE).
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: You can never guess an energy lower than the true minimum, so lower is always better.
EXAMPLE: For H = Z and |ψ(θ)⟩ above, E(θ) = cos θ ≥ −1 = E₀ (E04).
EQUATION: Resource estimate comparison — physical qubits 20,000,000 (2019) → under 1,000,000 (2025)
NAME: Change in estimated qubits needed for RSA-2048 (Gidney)
MEANING: Algorithmic and error-correction improvements reduced the estimate by roughly 20×, with the runtime rising from about 8 hours to under a week.
VARIABLES: Same assumptions in both: 0.1% gate error, 1 µs surface-code cycle, 10 µs reaction time, square grid with nearest-neighbour connections.
WHY IT MATTERS: Shows that estimates move, and not only with hardware progress.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Better recipes can cut the required hardware dramatically.
definitions: 8. Important Definitions
TERM: Shor's algorithm
DEFINITION: A quantum algorithm that factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time.
BEGINNER VERSION: The quantum recipe that could break RSA-style encryption on a big enough machine.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C01, C02
TERM: Grover's algorithm
DEFINITION: A quantum algorithm that finds a marked item among N unstructured items in about √N steps; optimal for unstructured search.
BEGINNER VERSION: A faster way (by a square root) to search a list with no structure.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C01, C05
TERM: Public-key cryptography
DEFINITION: Cryptography using a public key to encrypt or verify and a private key to decrypt or sign (e.g. RSA, elliptic-curve schemes).
BEGINNER VERSION: Locks anyone can close, but only the key owner can open.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C02
TERM: Symmetric cryptography
DEFINITION: Cryptography where the same secret key encrypts and decrypts (e.g. AES).
BEGINNER VERSION: One shared secret key for both locking and unlocking.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C02
TERM: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC)
DEFINITION: Classical cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks by both classical and quantum computers.
BEGINNER VERSION: New ordinary-computer encryption that a quantum computer should not break.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C03
TERM: Quantum key distribution (QKD)
DEFINITION: A method that uses quantum states, such as photons, to establish shared keys with detectable eavesdropping; BB84 is the first protocol.
BEGINNER VERSION: Using quantum physics to share a secret key safely.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C03
TERM: Harvest now, decrypt later
DEFINITION: An attack strategy of recording encrypted data now to decrypt it once a capable quantum computer exists.
BEGINNER VERSION: Stealing locked boxes today to open them with a future tool.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C02
TERM: Hamiltonian
DEFINITION: The mathematical operator that represents the total energy of a quantum system.
BEGINNER VERSION: The "energy rulebook" of a molecule or material.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C04
TERM: Variational quantum eigensolver (VQE)
DEFINITION: A hybrid algorithm that adjusts the parameters of a quantum circuit to minimise the measured energy of a Hamiltonian.
BEGINNER VERSION: A quantum–classical loop that tunes a circuit until its energy is as low as possible.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C04, C07
TERM: Quantum phase estimation (QPE)
DEFINITION: A quantum algorithm that estimates eigenvalues (such as energies) of a unitary operator; central to fault-tolerant chemistry algorithms.
BEGINNER VERSION: A method for reading out a system's energy very precisely on a fault-tolerant machine.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C04
TERM: NISQ (noisy intermediate-scale quantum)
DEFINITION: The class of current quantum devices with limited qubit counts and no full error correction.
BEGINNER VERSION: Today's small, error-prone quantum computers.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C08
TERM: Fault-tolerant quantum computing / logical qubit
DEFINITION: Computation protected by quantum error correction, where a logical qubit is encoded across many physical qubits so errors can be detected and corrected.
BEGINNER VERSION: A reliable "virtual" qubit made of many fragile real ones.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C08
TERM: Quantum advantage
DEFINITION: Solving a task that is beyond the reach of the best classical methods, ideally with the result verified and the task practically relevant.
BEGINNER VERSION: A quantum computer clearly beating the best classical approach.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C01, C08

activities: 10. Hands-On Activities
ACTIVITY ID: A01
TITLE: Sort the problems and read the headline
OBJECTIVE: Practise classifying applications and spotting hype.

STARTING STATE: A list of eight problems: factoring a 2048-bit number; computing a small molecule's energy; searching an unsorted list of a million entries; routing delivery trucks; training an image classifier; web browsing; breaking AES-256 by brute force; simulating a weather system.
STEPS:
1. Place each problem on the speedup ladder (V01): super-polynomial, quadratic, heuristic/unproven, or none expected.
2. For the headline "Quantum computer solves logistics problem 1000× faster", tick the V06 checklist: data loading? read-out? classical baseline? hardware?
3. Fill in one row of the readiness map (V08).

EXPECTED OBSERVATION: Factoring → super-polynomial; molecule → natural quantum case; search → quadratic; routing/image classifier → unproven; web browsing, weather → none expected; AES-256 → quadratic only.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: Speedups depend on problem structure, not on how "big" the problem sounds.
TRY THIS: Add two problems of your own and justify their placement.
EXPECTED RESULT: As in the observation above (deterministic classification).
OPEN QUESTION: What would you need to know about the logistics headline before believing it?
ACTIVITY ID: A02
TITLE: Grover vs classical counter
OBJECTIVE: See how the √N gap grows with N.
STARTING STATE: N = 16.
STEPS:
1. Run the Grover animation (V05) for N = 16 and record the number of iterations.
2. Repeat for N = 64 and N = 256.
3. Compare with the expected classical average N/2.
4. Compute (π/4)√N by hand for each N.
EXPECTED OBSERVATION: Grover's iterations grow roughly in proportion to √N.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: Each iteration increases the marked item's amplitude by a roughly fixed amount; the needed total grows like √N.
TRY THIS: What happens if you run too many iterations?
EXPECTED RESULT: (π/4)√N ≈ 3.1 for N = 16, ≈ 6.3 for N = 64, ≈ 12.6 for N = 256 (the animation will use whole numbers, e.g. 3, 6, 13).
OPEN QUESTION: At what point might the extra cost per quantum step cancel the √N advantage?
ACTIVITY ID: A03
TITLE: Key-strength calculator and PQC/QKD sorting
OBJECTIVE: Apply Shor/Grover correctly and separate PQC from QKD.
STARTING STATE: Calculator with key lengths 128, 192, 256 bits and a list of schemes.
STEPS:
1. For each symmetric key length k, compute 2^(k/2) as the idealised Grover cost.
2. Mark RSA-2048 and ECC as "broken by large quantum computer".
3. Sort these statements into PQC, QKD or both: "runs on normal servers", "uses photons", "standardised by NIST in 2024", "needs special links".
EXPECTED OBSERVATION: 128 → 2⁶⁴; 192 → 2⁹⁶; 256 → 2¹²⁸; "runs on normal servers" and "standardised by NIST in 2024" → PQC; "uses photons" and "needs special links" → QKD.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: Grover halves exponents; PQC and QKD are different technologies.

TRY THIS: Why might NIST still treat AES-128 as acceptable in practice even though Grover reduces it to 2⁶⁴? (Hint: Grover's steps cannot be easily parallelised and are expensive on error-corrected hardware; the tutor should present this as a view, not a proof.)
EXPECTED RESULT: As above (deterministic).
OPEN QUESTION: Why does doubling the key length restore the original quantum-era security level?
ACTIVITY ID: A04
TITLE: Toy variational loop
OBJECTIVE: Experience the hybrid optimisation loop.
STARTING STATE: One qubit, Hamiltonian H = Z, trial state with angle θ = 0.
STEPS:
1. Set θ = 0 and measure 1000 shots; compute E = P(0) − P(1).
2. Increase θ in steps (π/4, π/2, 3π/4, π) and repeat.
3. Plot E versus θ.
4. Let the optimiser (V07) find θ automatically.
EXPECTED OBSERVATION: E follows cos θ, with sampling noise; the optimiser settles near θ = π with E ≈ −1.
WHY THIS HAPPENS: E(θ) = cos θ (E04); the minimum equals the ground-state energy.
TRY THIS: Reduce shots to 10 and see how noisy the optimiser becomes.
EXPECTED RESULT: Ideal values E(0) = +1, E(π/4) ≈ +0.707, E(π/2) = 0, E(3π/4) ≈ −0.707, E(π) = −1.
OPEN QUESTION: Why does this toy problem not need a quantum computer, and what changes for molecules with many qubits?

full_topic_source_text: TOPIC 1.3 — QUANTUM COMPUTING APPLICATIONS

Source material for the QuantumLearnAI knowledge pack. Same structure and notation as Topic 1.2. Time-sensitivity warning: this topic mixes stable material (what algorithms do, why) with fast-changing material (hardware status, advantage claims, standards timelines). Every fast-changing fact is tagged TIME-SENSITIVE in Section 14 with the date it was checked (1 October 2026). The tutor must present those as "as of <date>" and must not present them as permanent. Verification note: numerical results (Grover iteration counts, key-size effects, the variational toy example) were derived by hand; confirm in the project simulator/calculator before release. Time-sensitive facts were checked against the sources in Section 16 on the date above. Syllabus assumption: Topic 1.2 introduces qubits, superposition, interference, entanglement, measurement, 2ⁿ amplitudes, and the idea that quantum speedups are problem-specific. Topic 1.3 applies these ideas and does not re-teach them.
1. Topic Metadata
TOPIC ID:
TOPIC TITLE:
Quantum Computing Applications
CATEGORY:
Quantum Computing Fundamentals
DIFFICULTY:
Beginner
ESTIMATED LEARNING TIME:
35–45 minutes
PREREQUISITES:
- Topic 1.1
- Topic 1.2 (qubits, superposition, interference, 2ⁿ amplitudes, "speedups are problem-specific")
- Basic familiarity with the idea of encryption (keys, "secure" vs "breakable")
SHORT DESCRIPTION:

This topic surveys what quantum computers are expected to be used for: breaking certain kinds of encryption, simulating quantum systems such as molecules and materials, speeding up some kinds of search and sampling, and (more speculatively) optimization and machine learning. For each area it explains why a quantum approach might help, what the evidence is, and how far today's hardware is from delivering. It also introduces post-quantum cryptography, the classical response to the cryptographic threat.
LEARNING OBJECTIVES:
By the end of this topic, the learner should be able to:
1. Name four major application areas of quantum computing and explain, for each, which quantum property or algorithm is the reason a speedup is expected.
2. Explain why Shor's algorithm threatens RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, and why Grover's algorithm is a much smaller threat to symmetric encryption.
3. Calculate how Grover's √N scaling changes the effective strength of a symmetric key and the number of steps for a given search size.
4. Explain why simulating molecules and materials is considered the most natural application of quantum computers.
5. Distinguish post-quantum cryptography from quantum key distribution.
6. Classify a proposed application as "strong theoretical case", "heuristic / unproven", or "unlikely to benefit", and justify the classification.
7. Describe the difference between today's noisy devices and the fault-tolerant machines that most large-scale applications need, and explain why "quantum advantage" claims must be read carefully.
2. Topic Overview
2.1 What is this topic?

Topic 1.2 showed that quantum computers are specialised machines: they help only when a problem's structure lets interference concentrate probability on correct answers. Topic 1.3 asks the practical question: which problems are those, and where do things stand?

Four areas dominate the discussion. Cryptography: Shor's algorithm would let a large, error-corrected quantum computer break the public-key systems (RSA, elliptic-curve cryptography) that protect most internet traffic today. The response, post-quantum cryptography (PQC), is a new set of classical algorithms believed to resist quantum attack, and standards for them already exist. Simulation: nature is quantum, so molecules and materials are natural targets; a quantum computer can represent a quantum system's state without the exponential memory cost a classical computer pays (Topic 1.2, C06). Search and sampling: Grover's algorithm gives a provable but only quadratic speedup for unstructured search, and related techniques give quadratic speedups for some estimation tasks. Optimization and machine learning: these are heavily advertised, but clear, proven speedups for practical problems are much rarer, and many claims are still being tested.

Two realities frame everything. First, almost all of the big applications need fault-tolerant quantum computers — machines far larger and more reliable than the noisy devices available now. Second, in this fast-moving field claims of "quantum advantage" are regularly challenged by improved classical algorithms. A good learner knows what is proven, what is plausible, and what is hype.
2.2 Why does it matter?

Why the learner needs this: it turns the abstract ideas of Topics 1.1–1.2 into concrete reasons to care about quantum computing, and it protects against both over-hype ("quantum solves everything") and over-dismissal ("it's all fake").
Where it fits: it closes the introductory unit. Later topics on gates, circuits and algorithms (e.g. Grover, Shor) will point back to the applications here as motivation.

Connection to Topics 1.1–1.2: 1.2 introduced the capabilities (superposition, interference, entanglement, exponential state space) and the limits (measurement returns n bits; no known efficient solution to NP-complete problems). 1.3 maps those capabilities and limits onto real problems.

After this topic the learner can: explain the "quantum threat" to encryption accurately, say why chemistry is the flagship use case, estimate Grover speedups, and critically read news about quantum advantage.
2.3 Prerequisite recap
Before learning Topic 1.3, remember:
• n qubits are described by 2ⁿ amplitudes, but measuring returns only n classical bits.
• Interference lets algorithms make correct answers more likely before measurement.
• Quantum speedups are problem-specific: Shor (factoring) is believed to be a large speedup;
Grover (unstructured search) is quadratic and provably optimal for that task.
• No efficient quantum algorithm for NP-complete problems is known.
• Today's quantum devices are noisy; large reliable computations need error correction.
3. Concepts
CONCEPT 1
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Where Quantum Speedups Come From (and the Types of Speedup)
What is it?
A framework for judging any application: a quantum algorithm may give an exponential-type speedup, a quadratic speedup, or no speedup, and the type decides whether it can matter in practice.
Why does it matter?

"Quantum is faster" is meaningless without saying how much faster, for what, and on what hardware. A quadratic speedup on a slow, error-corrected machine may never beat a fast classical one; a super-polynomial speedup can change what is computable.
How does it work?
Speedups are measured by how the number of steps grows with problem size N (or n bits). Types:
• Super-polynomial ("exponential-type"): e.g. Shor's factoring versus the best known classical factoring algorithms.
• Quadratic: e.g. Grover search, ~√N steps instead of ~N.
• Heuristic / no proven speedup: e.g. most optimization and machine-learning proposals; they may work well in practice, but nothing guarantees it.
Practical benefit also depends on overheads: error correction, clock speed, loading data in, and reading results out.
Visual explanation:
A "speedup ladder": three rungs labelled super-polynomial, quadratic, heuristic, each with example problems, and a second axis showing "hardware needed" (small noisy → large fault-tolerant).
Technical explanation:
Speedups are stated against the best known (or best possible) classical algorithm, and for some tasks (e.g. factoring) the classical comparison is "best known", not "proven optimal".
Mathematical representation:
Classical unstructured search ≈ N steps; Grover ≈ √N steps.
Factoring n-bit numbers: Shor ≈ polynomial in n; best known classical ≈ super-polynomial in n.
Example:
Doubling a problem's size doubles classical search time (~N) but multiplies Grover's time by only about √2.
Common mistake:
Treating all quantum speedups as "exponential". Most proven ones in search are quadratic.
Connection to previous concepts:
Extends Topic 1.2 C08 (what quantum computers are good at).
Try it:
Place example problems on the speedup ladder (Activity A01).
Key takeaway:
Ask three questions of any claimed application: how big is the speedup, against what classical method, and on what kind of hardware?
CONCEPT 2
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Cryptography: Shor's Algorithm and the Quantum Threat
What is it?

Shor's algorithm factors large integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time on an ideal quantum computer. Common public-key systems — RSA, Diffie–Hellman, and elliptic-curve cryptography — rely on these problems being hard for classical computers, so a large fault-tolerant quantum computer would break them.
Why does it matter?

Public-key cryptography secures web connections, software updates, digital signatures and certificates. Data encrypted today could be recorded now and decrypted later once a capable quantum computer exists ("harvest now, decrypt later"), which makes migration planning urgent even before such a machine exists.
How does it work?

Shor's algorithm reduces factoring to finding the period of a function; a quantum computer finds that period efficiently using superposition and interference (the Quantum Fourier Transform), which Topic 1.2 C05 previewed. Classical computers have no known efficient method.
Important limits:

• It requires a large, error-corrected quantum computer. A 2025 resource estimate by Gidney (Google Quantum AI) says factoring a 2048-bit RSA number could take fewer than one million noisy physical qubits and under a week, under stated assumptions (0.1% gate error, surface-code cycle of 1 µs, 10 µs reaction time). That is roughly 20× fewer qubits than the 2019 estimate of about 20 million qubits and 8 hours. It is an estimate, not a demonstration, and no machine of that size and quality exists today.
• Symmetric ciphers (e.g. AES) and hash functions are not broken by Shor. Grover's algorithm only provides a square-root speedup for brute-force key search.
Visual explanation:
Two columns: "Broken by Shor (large fault-tolerant quantum computer)": RSA, Diffie–Hellman, ECC. "Weakened only quadratically by Grover": AES, SHA-family hashes (mitigate with longer keys/outputs).
Technical explanation:
Shor's algorithm runs in time polynomial in the number of bits; the best known classical factoring algorithm (the general number field sieve) is sub-exponential but super-polynomial.
Mathematical representation:
Grover on a k-bit key: ~2^(k/2) steps instead of ~2^k.
AES-128: ~2¹²⁸ → ~2⁶⁴ (idealised); AES-256: ~2²⁵⁶ → ~2¹²⁸.
Example:
See E02: how Shor and Grover affect RSA, ECC, AES-128 and AES-256.
Common mistake:
Saying "quantum computers will break all encryption". Only certain public-key schemes are broken; symmetric encryption just needs larger keys.
Connection to previous concepts:
Applies Topic 1.2's interference idea and its note that Shor's algorithm gives a large speedup while Grover's is quadratic.
Try it:
Use the key-strength calculator (Activity A03) to compare classical and quantum-attack strength.
Key takeaway:
Shor's algorithm threatens public-key cryptography; Grover's algorithm only halves the effective bit-strength of symmetric keys. No machine capable of breaking RSA-2048 exists today.
CONCEPT 3
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)
What is it?

PQC means classical cryptographic algorithms designed to stay secure against both classical and quantum attackers. QKD is a different idea: using quantum physics to distribute encryption keys, which needs quantum hardware and communication links.
Why does it matter?

PQC is the main practical response to the quantum threat, and it runs on today's ordinary computers. Learners often confuse it with QKD, or think defending against quantum computers requires a quantum computer.
How does it work?

PQC schemes rely on mathematical problems with no known efficient quantum attack (for example problems on lattices, hash functions or error-correcting codes). NIST published its first PQC standards in August 2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, key establishment), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, signatures) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, hash-based signatures). A further signature standard (FIPS 206, based on FALCON) was still in development at the time of checking, and NIST selected HQC in March 2025 as an additional key-establishment algorithm. QKD (the first protocol is BB84, 1984) uses quantum states to establish keys whose eavesdropping can be detected, but it needs specialised hardware and still requires classical authentication.
Visual explanation:
A comparison diagram: PQC = new maths, runs on normal computers, software upgrade; QKD = quantum hardware and links, physics-based key exchange.
Technical explanation:

PQC security is based on computational hardness assumptions (not proven unconditionally); algorithms undergo years of public cryptanalysis, and some candidates have been broken classically in the past, which is why standardisation is slow and cautious.
Mathematical representation:
None required (conceptual).
Example:
A web server can adopt ML-KEM for key exchange through a software update; no quantum hardware is involved.
Common mistake:
Thinking "post-quantum" means "uses quantum computers" or that PQC and QKD are the same thing.
Connection to previous concepts:
Follows directly from C02.
Try it:
Sort statements into "PQC", "QKD", or "both" (Activity A03, part 2).
Key takeaway:
Post-quantum cryptography is classical software designed to resist quantum attacks; it is available as standards today. QKD is a separate, hardware-based approach.
CONCEPT 4
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Simulating Quantum Systems: Chemistry and Materials
What is it?
Using a quantum computer to model the behaviour of molecules, catalysts, and materials — for example to compute their energy levels — directly with quantum states.
Why does it matter?

This is widely regarded as the most natural application: the idea goes back to Richard Feynman in the early 1980s, who argued that simulating quantum physics on classical computers is inefficient while a quantum computer could do it naturally. Better simulation could help with understanding catalysts, batteries, drug-target interactions and new materials.
How does it work?

The state of a quantum system with n relevant quantum degrees of freedom needs ~2ⁿ amplitudes on a classical computer (Topic 1.2 C06). A quantum computer with roughly n qubits (in standard encodings, about one qubit per electronic orbital state) can hold such a state natively. Algorithms such as quantum phase estimation can compute ground-state energies with provable guarantees on fault-tolerant hardware; **hybrid variational algorithms** such as the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) use short noisy circuits plus a classical optimiser and are designed for current devices, but their advantage over classical methods is unproven.

Honest status: small molecules have been simulated on quantum hardware; useful, classically-intractable chemistry is expected to need fault-tolerant machines. Resource estimates for practically relevant molecules vary by orders of magnitude, and improved classical methods keep raising the bar quantum computers must clear.
Visual explanation:
A molecule on the left with its electron orbitals; on the right, qubits representing orbitals; a growing "classical memory needed" bar versus a "qubits needed" bar.
Technical explanation:
The goal is typically the ground-state energy of a Hamiltonian H. The variational principle guarantees that any trial state's energy is ≥ the true ground-state energy, which VQE exploits.
Mathematical representation:
E(θ) = ⟨ψ(θ)| H |ψ(θ)⟩ ≥ E₀ ;  VQE minimises E(θ) over θ.
Example:
See E03 (state-space size) and E04 (a one-qubit variational toy example).
Common mistake:
Saying "quantum computers can simulate anything faster". The natural advantage is for quantum systems; many classical systems (weather, traffic) have no known quantum speedup.
Connection to previous concepts:
Directly applies the 2ⁿ state-space growth from Topic 1.2.
Try it:
Slide the number of orbitals and compare classical memory with qubit count (Visual V04), then run the toy variational loop (Activity A04).
Key takeaway:
Simulating quantum systems is the strongest, most natural application case, but useful large-scale results are expected to need fault-tolerant quantum computers.
CONCEPT 5
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Search, Sampling and Estimation (Grover and Relatives)
What is it?

Grover's algorithm finds a marked item among N unsorted items in about √N steps; related "amplitude amplification/estimation" methods give a similar quadratic speedup for some counting and Monte Carlo estimation tasks.
Why does it matter?
Searching a huge space is common (cryptanalysis, constraint problems, estimation in finance and science). A quadratic speedup is real but modest, and overheads can erase it.
How does it work?

Grover's algorithm repeatedly applies two steps that, through interference, raise the amplitude of the marked item while lowering the others (Topic 1.2 C05, M02). It is provably optimal: no quantum algorithm can do unstructured search faster than order √N.

Practical caveats: (a) the speedup is only quadratic; (b) error correction makes each quantum step much more expensive than a classical step; (c) the "oracle" that recognises the right answer must itself be implemented as a circuit; (d) if the search space has structure, a classical algorithm may beat brute force by far more than √N.
Visual explanation:
A bar chart of amplitudes: initially all equal, then the marked item's bar grows over repeated iterations (animation), with an iteration counter next to a classical "checks so far" counter.
Technical explanation:
For one marked item among N, about (π/4)√N Grover iterations are needed; stopping too early or too late reduces the success probability.
Mathematical representation:
Iterations ≈ (π/4)·√N ;  classical expected checks ≈ N/2 (worst case N).
Example:
See E01: N = 1,000,000 → about 785 Grover iterations versus about 500,000 expected classical checks.
Common mistake:
Thinking Grover's algorithm makes NP-complete problems easy. It reduces brute-force search time by a square root, which is still exponential for exponentially large search spaces.
Connection to previous concepts:
Builds on interference (Topic 1.2 C05) and the "tries all possibilities" misconception (M02).
Try it:
Use the Grover-vs-classical slider (Activity A02).
Key takeaway:
Grover gives a proven but quadratic speedup for unstructured search; it is useful, but not a magic key to hard problems.
CONCEPT 6
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Optimization and Machine Learning: Promise vs Proof
What is it?

Optimization (logistics, scheduling, portfolio choice) and machine learning are frequently cited as quantum applications. Approaches include quantum annealing, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), and quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms.
Why does it matter?
These areas get the most commercial attention, so learners need to separate demonstrated results from marketing. Being cautious here is a sign of understanding, not pessimism.
How does it work?

• Optimization: heuristic quantum methods (QAOA, annealing) explore solutions using superposition and interference, but there is no general proof that they beat the best classical heuristics on practical problems. Because NP-hard optimization problems are not known to be efficiently solvable by quantum computers, any gain is expected to be limited (e.g. quadratic, or heuristic and instance-specific).

• Machine learning: some proposed QML algorithms promise large speedups, but these often depend on assumptions that are hard to satisfy: loading classical data into a quantum state can itself take as long as the computation; reading results out gives limited information; and several proposed speedups were later matched by new classical ("dequantised") algorithms, e.g. for recommendation systems.
• Estimation: amplitude-estimation methods give a quadratic speedup in some Monte Carlo estimation tasks, relevant in principle to finance, but needing large fault-tolerant machines.
Visual explanation:
A "claim checklist" graphic: data in → quantum algorithm → result out, with warning icons on the data-loading and read-out steps; alongside a column "classical baseline improved?".
Technical explanation:
The "fine print" principle: a quantum speedup claim must be checked for input cost, output cost, the classical baseline used, and the hardware assumed.
Mathematical representation:
None required.
Example:
A paper claims a quantum algorithm solves a linear-algebra step exponentially faster; but if the input matrix must be loaded entry by entry, the loading time can dominate and remove the advantage.
Common mistake:
Assuming quantum computers will train neural networks or solve logistics problems "exponentially faster".
Connection to previous concepts:
Applies the limits stated in Topic 1.2 (M02–M04) to concrete application claims.
Try it:
Use the claim-checklist activity (A01, part 2) on a made-up headline.
Key takeaway:
For optimization and machine learning, quantum advantage is an open research question; judge claims by the fine print.
CONCEPT 7
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Hybrid Quantum–Classical Computing
What is it?

Most practical quantum workflows pair a quantum processor with classical computers (CPUs/GPUs/supercomputers). The classical side prepares inputs, optimises parameters, processes results and applies error mitigation; the quantum side runs the parts it is suited for.
Why does it matter?
Quantum computers will not replace classical computers (Topic 1.2). They are expected to act as accelerators for specific sub-tasks, much as GPUs are today.
How does it work?

Variational algorithms (VQE, QAOA) loop: the classical optimiser proposes parameters θ → the quantum computer prepares a state and measures many shots → the classical computer updates θ. Even fault-tolerant machines need heavy classical processing for error-correction decoding and for pre-/post-processing.
Visual explanation:
A loop diagram with a "classical optimiser" box and a "quantum processor" box connected by arrows labelled "parameters θ" and "measurement results".
Technical explanation:
Noisy-device workflows trade circuit depth for repeated runs and classical post-processing.
Mathematical representation:
θ_(k+1) = Optimiser(θ_k, E(θ_k)), where E(θ) is estimated from measured shots.
Example:
E04's one-qubit example is a miniature variational loop.
Common mistake:
Imagining a quantum computer as a standalone replacement for a data centre.
Connection to previous concepts:
Reinforces Topic 1.2: quantum devices are specialised, noisy, and probabilistic (many shots needed).
Try it:
Run the variational loop in A04 and watch the energy fall to its minimum.
Key takeaway:
Practical quantum computing is hybrid: classical computers do most of the work and call on quantum processors for specific tasks.
CONCEPT 8
Concept ID:
Concept Title:
Readiness: Noisy Devices, Fault Tolerance, and Reading "Quantum Advantage" Claims
What is it?

A way to judge how close each application is to reality: today's devices are noisy and limited; large, reliable (fault-tolerant) machines are needed for most high-value applications; "quantum advantage" claims must be read carefully.
Why does it matter?
Applications are often described as if hardware were already ready. Learners should know the gap and the reasons progress is real yet uncertain.
How does it work?
• Noisy intermediate-scale ("NISQ") devices: tens to hundreds or more of physical qubits with errors that limit circuit size. Useful for experiments, benchmarks and algorithm research.

• Fault-tolerant devices: many physical qubits combine into each error-corrected logical qubit. Experiments have shown that making the error-correcting code larger can reduce the logical error rate (the "below threshold" result, Google Quantum AI), and in 2026 IBM and collaborators reported a computation using 70 logical qubits. These are milestones, not yet the machines needed for Shor-scale factoring or large-scale chemistry.

• "Quantum advantage" means a quantum computer solves some task beyond the reach of the best classical methods. Claims are tested by new classical algorithms, and some have been narrowed or challenged after publication (the 2019 Google "supremacy" experiment was followed by improved classical simulations). Strong claims therefore need verification that the quantum result is correct and a comparison with the best classical baselines. Advantage on a contrived benchmark is not the same as useful advantage on a real-world problem.
Visual explanation:

A readiness map: application areas (columns) against hardware stages (noisy today / early fault-tolerant / large fault-tolerant), with shading for "demonstrated small-scale", "plausible", "needs large machine".
Technical explanation:

Physical qubits have error rates far above what long algorithms require; error correction encodes one logical qubit in many physical qubits and corrects errors continuously. The overhead, not just the algorithm, sets feasibility.
Mathematical representation:
None required.
Example:

Resource estimates for factoring 2048-bit RSA fell about 20-fold in six years (from ~20 million to under one million physical qubits) mainly because of algorithm and error-correction improvements, not new hardware, which shows why timelines are uncertain in both directions.
Common mistake:
Treating a headline ("quantum advantage achieved!") as proof that quantum computers are now useful for business or that RSA is broken.
Connection to previous concepts:

5. Worked Examples
EXAMPLE ID: E01
TITLE: Grover versus classical search for one million items
RELATED CONCEPT: C05
GOAL: Quantify the quadratic speedup.
GIVEN: N = 1,000,000 unsorted items, exactly one marked item.
STEP 1: Classical random search: on average it checks about N/2 items; worst case N.
STEP 2: Grover: about (π/4)·√N iterations.
STEP 3: Compute √N and the iteration count.
CALCULATION:
Grover iterations ≈ (π/4) × 1,000 ≈ 785
Classical expected checks ≈ 1,000,000 / 2 = 500,000
RESULT: ≈ 785 Grover iterations vs ≈ 500,000 expected classical checks.
INTERPRETATION: A big reduction in the number of steps, but the comparison ignores how expensive each fault-tolerant quantum step is, and the cost of building the oracle.
COMMON MISTAKE: Saying Grover needs "1 step" or "log N steps"; it needs about √N.
TRY YOURSELF: For N = 100, how many Grover iterations? (Answer: (π/4)×10 ≈ 7.85, i.e. about 8.)
EXAMPLE ID: E02
TITLE: Which cryptography is affected, and how?
RELATED CONCEPT: C02, C03
GOAL: Apply Shor and Grover correctly to real schemes.
GIVEN: RSA-2048, elliptic-curve cryptography, AES-128, AES-256.
STEP 1: Identify the hard problem each scheme relies on.
STEP 2: Decide whether Shor applies (factoring / discrete logarithms) or only Grover (brute-force key search).
STEP 3: For Grover cases, halve the exponent of the key space.
CALCULATION:
RSA-2048: factoring → Shor applies → broken by a large fault-tolerant quantum computer.
ECC: elliptic-curve discrete logarithm → Shor-type algorithm applies → broken by such a machine.
AES-128: key space 2¹²⁸ → Grover ≈ 2⁶⁴ steps (idealised).
AES-256: key space 2²⁵⁶ → Grover ≈ 2¹²⁸ steps (idealised).
RESULT: Public-key schemes are broken in principle; AES-256 retains about 128-bit quantum strength.
INTERPRETATION: The fix for symmetric encryption is larger keys; the fix for public-key encryption is new algorithms (PQC).
COMMON MISTAKE: Saying AES is "broken" by quantum computers, or that Grover makes AES-256 weaker than classical AES-128 (it does not).
TRY YOURSELF: What is the Grover-equivalent strength of a 192-bit symmetric key? (Answer: about 96 bits.)
EXAMPLE ID: E03
TITLE: Why molecules are hard to simulate classically
RELATED CONCEPT: C04
GOAL: Connect molecule size to state-space growth.
GIVEN: A molecular model with n electronic orbital states, using roughly one qubit per orbital state (illustrative standard encoding).
STEP 1: Number of qubits ≈ n.
STEP 2: Classical full-state description needs 2ⁿ amplitudes.
STEP 3: At 16 bytes per amplitude, estimate memory.
CALCULATION:
n = 30 → 2³⁰ = 1,073,741,824 amplitudes → ×16 bytes = 2³⁴ bytes = 16 GiB
n = 50 → 2⁵⁰ = 1,125,899,906,842,624 amplitudes → ×16 bytes = 2⁵⁴ bytes = 16 PiB
RESULT: A 30-orbital model fits in a large workstation's memory; a 50-orbital model does not fit on any ordinary machine if stored as a full state vector.
INTERPRETATION: This is why brute-force classical simulation of larger molecules fails, and why clever classical approximations (and, in the future, quantum computers) are used.
COMMON MISTAKE: Concluding that classical computers can never simulate such systems. Classical approximation methods work very well for many molecules; the open question is the hard cases.
TRY YOURSELF: How much memory does n = 40 need at 16 bytes per amplitude? (Answer: 2⁴⁴ bytes = 16 TiB.)
EXAMPLE ID: E04
TITLE: A one-qubit variational loop (toy VQE)
RELATED CONCEPT: C04, C07
GOAL: Show the variational idea with a checkable calculation.
GIVEN: Hamiltonian H = Z (eigenvalues +1 for |0⟩ and −1 for |1⟩; so the true ground-state energy is E₀ = −1). Trial state |ψ(θ)⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + sin(θ/2)|1⟩.
STEP 1: Write the energy E(θ) = ⟨ψ|Z|ψ⟩ = P(0)·(+1) + P(1)·(−1).
STEP 2: Insert P(0) = cos²(θ/2), P(1) = sin²(θ/2).
STEP 3: Simplify and find the minimum over θ.
CALCULATION:
E(θ) = cos²(θ/2) − sin²(θ/2) = cos θ
RESULT: The minimum is E = −1 at θ = π, where |ψ⟩ = |1⟩; this equals E₀.
INTERPRETATION: The "quantum" part is estimating E(θ) from measurement shots; the "classical" part is choosing θ to lower the energy. Real VQE does the same with many qubits and parameters.
COMMON MISTAKE: Believing the optimiser "knows" the answer; it only sees estimated energies and nudges θ.
TRY YOURSELF: With 1000 shots at θ = π/2, what is the expected estimate of E? (Answer: about 0, with statistical spread of roughly ±0.03.)

6. Mathematical Foundations
EQUATION: Iterations ≈ (π/4)·√N
NAME: Grover iteration count (one marked item)
MEANING: Approximate number of Grover iterations to find one marked item among N.
VARIABLES: N = size of the search space.
WHY IT MATTERS: Quantifies the quadratic speedup.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Search time grows like the square root of the list size instead of the list size.
EQUATION: Effective quantum search cost of a k-bit key ≈ 2^(k/2)
NAME: Grover effect on symmetric keys (idealised)
MEANING: A k-bit key space of size 2ᵏ is searched in about 2^(k/2) steps.
VARIABLES: k = key length in bits.
WHY IT MATTERS: Explains why doubling key length restores security against Grover.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: The attacker's work is halved in the exponent; a 256-bit key behaves like a 128-bit key.
EXAMPLE: AES-256 → ≈ 2¹²⁸ (E02).
EQUATION: Number of amplitudes = 2ⁿ ;  memory ≈ 2ⁿ × 16 bytes (double-precision complex)
NAME: State-vector size
MEANING: Memory to store a general n-qubit state classically.
VARIABLES: n = number of qubits (or orbitals).
WHY IT MATTERS: Shows why direct classical simulation of larger quantum systems fails.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Each added qubit doubles the memory.
EXAMPLE: n = 50 → 16 PiB (E03).
EQUATION: E(θ) = ⟨ψ(θ)| H |ψ(θ)⟩ ≥ E₀
NAME: Variational principle
MEANING: Any trial state's average energy is at least the true lowest energy E₀.
VARIABLES: θ = adjustable parameters; H = Hamiltonian (energy operator); E₀ = ground-state energy.
WHY IT MATTERS: Justifies minimising E(θ) to approach the ground state (VQE).
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: You can never guess an energy lower than the true minimum, so lower is always better.
EXAMPLE: For H = Z and |ψ(θ)⟩ above, E(θ) = cos θ ≥ −1 = E₀ (E04).
EQUATION: Resource estimate comparison — physical qubits 20,000,000 (2019) → under 1,000,000 (2025)
NAME: Change in estimated qubits needed for RSA-2048 (Gidney)
MEANING: Algorithmic and error-correction improvements reduced the estimate by roughly 20×, with the runtime rising from about 8 hours to under a week.
VARIABLES: Same assumptions in both: 0.1% gate error, 1 µs surface-code cycle, 10 µs reaction time, square grid with nearest-neighbour connections.
WHY IT MATTERS: Shows that estimates move, and not only with hardware progress.
BEGINNER INTERPRETATION: Better recipes can cut the required hardware dramatically.
7. Common Misconceptions
MISCONCEPTION ID: M01
WRONG CLAIM: "Quantum computers can already break RSA / encryption is already broken."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: Headlines about "quantum advantage" and "quantum threat".

WHY IT IS WRONG: Breaking RSA-2048 needs a large fault-tolerant quantum computer. Published estimates are on the order of a million noisy physical qubits running for days; no such machine exists today.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "RSA is vulnerable in principle to a future large fault-tolerant quantum computer; no machine capable of breaking RSA-2048 exists today."
EXAMPLE: E02; Gidney 2025 is an estimate, not an attack.
TRIGGER WORDS: already broken, Q-Day happened, cracked RSA, breaks encryption today
MISCONCEPTION ID: M02
WRONG CLAIM: "Quantum computers will break all encryption, including AES."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: "Encryption" is treated as one thing.

WHY IT IS WRONG: Shor's algorithm targets factoring and discrete-logarithm-based public-key schemes. Symmetric ciphers like AES face only Grover's quadratic speedup, which halves the effective key length in the exponent.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "Public-key schemes such as RSA and ECC are threatened by Shor; symmetric ciphers remain secure with sufficiently long keys (e.g. 256-bit)."
EXAMPLE: AES-256 → ≈128-bit strength under Grover.
TRIGGER WORDS: all encryption, AES broken, everything, any cipher
MISCONCEPTION ID: M03
WRONG CLAIM: "Post-quantum cryptography needs a quantum computer" or "PQC and QKD are the same."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: The word "quantum" appears in both names.
WHY IT IS WRONG: PQC is classical algorithms (ordinary software) designed to resist quantum attacks. QKD uses quantum hardware and communication links, and is a different technology.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "PQC runs on classical computers; QKD uses quantum physics for key distribution."
EXAMPLE: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is software; BB84 is a quantum protocol.
TRIGGER WORDS: post-quantum, PQC, QKD, quantum encryption, needs quantum computer
MISCONCEPTION ID: M04
WRONG CLAIM: "Quantum computers will solve optimization problems like logistics exponentially faster."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: Many optimization problems have huge search spaces, which sounds like "try all possibilities".

WHY IT IS WRONG: No general exponential speedup for NP-hard optimization is known; proven results are at most quadratic (via Grover-type methods), and heuristic quantum methods have not been shown to beat the best classical heuristics in practice.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "Quantum optimization is an active research area; at best modest or instance-specific speedups are expected, and none is established for general practical problems."
EXAMPLE: See C06.
TRIGGER WORDS: optimization, logistics, scheduling, exponentially faster, solve NP-hard
MISCONCEPTION ID: M05
WRONG CLAIM: "Quantum machine learning will make AI training exponentially faster."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: Machine learning involves large linear algebra, which quantum algorithms can speed up in theory.
WHY IT IS WRONG: Speedups usually assume cheap data loading and limited read-out; loading classical data can erase the advantage, and several QML speedups were matched by new classical algorithms.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "QML claims depend on strong assumptions about data input and output; practical advantages for mainstream machine learning have not been established."
EXAMPLE: Recommendation-system algorithm matched by a classical "dequantised" algorithm.
TRIGGER WORDS: quantum AI, train neural networks, big data, quantum machine learning
MISCONCEPTION ID: M06
WRONG CLAIM: "Quantum computers can simulate anything faster, including everyday physical systems."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: "Simulation" sounds general.
WHY IT IS WRONG: The strong case is for simulating quantum systems. Many classical simulations (weather, traffic, most engineering) have no known quantum speedup.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "Quantum computers are expected to simulate quantum systems efficiently; there is no general speedup for classical simulation."
EXAMPLE: Chemistry vs weather forecasting.
TRIGGER WORDS: simulate anything, weather, simulation, faster physics
MISCONCEPTION ID: M07
WRONG CLAIM: "Quantum advantage has been achieved, so quantum computers are now useful for business."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: Press releases announce advantage milestones.
WHY IT IS WRONG: Advantage demonstrations so far are on specific, often contrived tasks, can be challenged by new classical methods, and do not by themselves show commercially useful results.

CORRECT STATEMENT: "Quantum advantage claims show quantum devices beating known classical methods on particular tasks; practical, useful advantage on real-world problems is still being demonstrated and debated."
EXAMPLE: The 2019 supremacy claim was followed by improved classical simulations.
TRIGGER WORDS: advantage achieved, supremacy, useful today, commercial value now
MISCONCEPTION ID: M08
WRONG CLAIM: "Quantum computing is all hype and will never work."
WHY IT SEEMS REASONABLE: Over-promising is common, and timelines have slipped.

WHY IT IS WRONG: Error-correction experiments have shown logical error rates falling as code size grows, and algorithmic resource estimates have dropped sharply. Large-scale usefulness is not guaranteed, but there is real, peer-reviewed progress.
CORRECT STATEMENT: "Progress is real but incomplete; most high-value applications depend on hardware that does not yet exist."
EXAMPLE: C08 (below-threshold error correction; resource estimates falling).
TRIGGER WORDS: hype, scam, never work, vapourware
8. Important Definitions
TERM: Shor's algorithm
DEFINITION: A quantum algorithm that factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time.
BEGINNER VERSION: The quantum recipe that could break RSA-style encryption on a big enough machine.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C01, C02
TERM: Grover's algorithm
DEFINITION: A quantum algorithm that finds a marked item among N unstructured items in about √N steps; optimal for unstructured search.
BEGINNER VERSION: A faster way (by a square root) to search a list with no structure.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C01, C05
TERM: Public-key cryptography
DEFINITION: Cryptography using a public key to encrypt or verify and a private key to decrypt or sign (e.g. RSA, elliptic-curve schemes).
BEGINNER VERSION: Locks anyone can close, but only the key owner can open.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C02
TERM: Symmetric cryptography
DEFINITION: Cryptography where the same secret key encrypts and decrypts (e.g. AES).
BEGINNER VERSION: One shared secret key for both locking and unlocking.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C02
TERM: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC)
DEFINITION: Classical cryptographic algorithms designed to resist attacks by both classical and quantum computers.
BEGINNER VERSION: New ordinary-computer encryption that a quantum computer should not break.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C03
TERM: Quantum key distribution (QKD)
DEFINITION: A method that uses quantum states, such as photons, to establish shared keys with detectable eavesdropping; BB84 is the first protocol.
BEGINNER VERSION: Using quantum physics to share a secret key safely.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C03
TERM: Harvest now, decrypt later
DEFINITION: An attack strategy of recording encrypted data now to decrypt it once a capable quantum computer exists.
BEGINNER VERSION: Stealing locked boxes today to open them with a future tool.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C02
TERM: Hamiltonian
DEFINITION: The mathematical operator that represents the total energy of a quantum system.
BEGINNER VERSION: The "energy rulebook" of a molecule or material.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C04
TERM: Variational quantum eigensolver (VQE)
DEFINITION: A hybrid algorithm that adjusts the parameters of a quantum circuit to minimise the measured energy of a Hamiltonian.
BEGINNER VERSION: A quantum–classical loop that tunes a circuit until its energy is as low as possible.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C04, C07
TERM: Quantum phase estimation (QPE)
DEFINITION: A quantum algorithm that estimates eigenvalues (such as energies) of a unitary operator; central to fault-tolerant chemistry algorithms.
BEGINNER VERSION: A method for reading out a system's energy very precisely on a fault-tolerant machine.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C04
TERM: NISQ (noisy intermediate-scale quantum)
DEFINITION: The class of current quantum devices with limited qubit counts and no full error correction.
BEGINNER VERSION: Today's small, error-prone quantum computers.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C08
TERM: Fault-tolerant quantum computing / logical qubit
DEFINITION: Computation protected by quantum error correction, where a logical qubit is encoded across many physical qubits so errors can be detected and corrected.
BEGINNER VERSION: A reliable "virtual" qubit made of many fragile real ones.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C08
TERM: Quantum advantage
DEFINITION: Solving a task that is beyond the reach of the best classical methods, ideally with the result verified and the task practically relevant.
BEGINNER VERSION: A quantum computer clearly beating the best classical approach.
RELATED CONCEPTS: C01, C08

17. Topic Summary
What you should now know
Quantum speedups come in different sizes: super-polynomial (Shor, versus the best known classical), quadratic (Grover), or unproven (most optimisation and machine-learning claims).
Shor's algorithm threatens RSA, Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve cryptography; Grover's algorithm only halves the exponent of symmetric key strength (AES-256 ≈ 128-bit under Grover).
Post-quantum cryptography is classical software that resists quantum attack; NIST published its first standards in August 2024. Quantum key distribution is a different, hardware-based technology.
Simulating molecules and materials is the strongest natural application, because a quantum state needs 2ⁿ amplitudes classically but about n qubits quantumly.
Practical workflows are hybrid: classical computers optimise and process while quantum processors run specific circuits (e.g. VQE).

Most high-value applications need fault-tolerant machines that do not yet exist at the required scale; "quantum advantage" claims must be checked for verification, classical baselines and real-world relevance.

Grover iterations ≈ (π/4)·√N
Effective Grover cost of a k-bit key ≈ 2^(k/2)
State-vector size = 2ⁿ amplitudes (≈ 2ⁿ × 16 bytes)
E(θ) = ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ ≥ E₀   (variational principle)
Toy example: H = Z → E(θ) = cos θ
